explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, "In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice…" (Psalm 5:3). Then he adds, "at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation." Morning and daybreak both show up in that one verse.

Evening was a solid guess, friend, and I'd have picked it too after a long day at the ovens. But David names a different time: "In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice…" (Psalm 5:3). He says "at daybreak" right after that, so this verse is about the sun coming up, not going down.

Midnight is when I do my best worrying, baker, so I get the pick. But David doesn't say midnight in this verse. He says, "In the morning, O LORD, You hear my voice…" (Psalm 5:3). His prayer rises with the day.

That's right, baker. David says, "at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation." (Psalm 5:3). Two steps: he lays out his plea, then he waits. It's a lot like putting a tray in the oven and not opening the door every four seconds. I still haven't mastered that part.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, "at daybreak I lay my plea before You and wait in expectation." (Psalm 5:3). David does both things: he brings his plea, and then he waits. The waiting isn't empty either, because he waits in expectation.
Not quite, friend. David says the opposite: "no evil can dwell with You." (Psalm 5:4). Not some evil, not a little evil, none. God's presence has no room for it.

Right, baker. David says God is not a God who delights in wickedness, and "no evil can dwell with You." (Psalm 5:4). That word "no" doesn't leave any gaps. So the answer is False, since David says none.

explanations.answer: The man of bloodshed and deceit
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. David says, "the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit." (Psalm 5:6). Right before that he says God destroys those who tell lies. David isn't listing people God dislikes for no reason. He's naming violence and lies.

explanations.answer: The man who is poor and needy
explanations.explanation: No, friend, and I'm glad that one isn't true. David names a different man: "the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit." (Psalm 5:6). Nothing in this verse says a word about people being poor or needy. The verse is about lies and violence.

explanations.answer: The man who is new in the land
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. Being the new guy is rough, believe me. But David says, "the LORD abhors the man of bloodshed and deceit." (Psalm 5:6). Being new has nothing to do with it.

explanations.answer: The great love God shows him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, "…I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion…" (Psalm 5:7). Notice whose love it is. It's God's love that gets him in, not David's résumé. That's good news for anyone who has ever shown up with a messy apron.

explanations.answer: The good deeds he has done
explanations.explanation: I understand why that one feels natural, friend. But David says, "…I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion…" (Psalm 5:7). He points to God's loving devotion, not to his own list. He doesn't mention his deeds at all.

explanations.answer: The offerings he brings to God
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, since a temple makes you think of offerings. But David says, "…I will enter Your house by the abundance of Your loving devotion…" (Psalm 5:7). What gets him in is God's loving devotion. Offerings don't come up in this verse.

That's right, baker. David prays, "make straight Your way before me." (Psalm 5:8). He's asking for God's way to be clear in front of him, not his own. When you know the road is God's, you can walk it with a lot less squinting.

Good guess, friend, but look at the word David uses. He prays, "make straight Your way before me." (Psalm 5:8). That's "Your," so it's the LORD's way, not David's own heart. He asks it right after "Lead me, O LORD, in Your righteousness…"

I get it, baker, because his enemies are right there in the verse. David says he asks the LORD to lead him "…because of my enemies…" But then he prays, "make straight Your way before me." (Psalm 5:8). It's God's way, not theirs.

Not quite, friend. David says the opposite: "…not a word they speak can be trusted…" (Psalm 5:9). That means not one word. Imagine getting a text from someone like that and not being able to believe a single letter of it.

Right, baker. David doesn't say most of their words can be trusted. He says, "…not a word they speak can be trusted…" (Psalm 5:9). Not most, not half, not one. Nothing in the verse leaves a single word standing.

You got it, baker. David asks God to drive them out "…for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You." (Psalm 5:10). The reason he gives is that they rebelled against God. He doesn't point to something they did to him.

I see why that sounds right, friend, but the psalm doesn't say it. David gives this reason: "…for they have rebelled against You." (Psalm 5:10). His reason is their rebellion against God. Stealing never comes up.

That's a big charge, baker, but the psalm never makes it. David asks God to drive them out "…for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You." (Psalm 5:10). A destroyed city isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses. The reason he gives is rebellion against God.

Yes, baker. David prays, "May You shelter them, that those who love Your name may rejoice in You." (Psalm 5:11). It's a request, and "shelter" is the word he picks for those who take refuge in God. It's a cozy word, like a warm kitchen on a cold night.

Good try, friend, but that's not the word in this verse. David says, "May You shelter them…" (Psalm 5:11). He's asking for shelter for those who take refuge in Him. That fits, because refuge and shelter go together.

Whoa, baker, scatter would be a sad thing to ask for people running to God for safety. David actually says, "May You shelter them…" (Psalm 5:11). He asks the LORD to shelter those who take refuge in Him, which is the opposite of scattering them.

That's right, baker. David says, "You surround them with the shield of Your favor." (Psalm 5:12). A shield goes all the way around here, and it's made of God's favor. That's about the best armor a person could ask for.

A sword is a soldier's tool, friend, so I see the thinking. But David says, "You surround them with the shield of Your favor." (Psalm 5:12). A sword is for swinging, while a shield is for covering. Here God's favor is the thing that surrounds His people.

Nice soldier thinking, baker, but a spear is pointed outward. David says, "You surround them with the shield of Your favor." (Psalm 5:12). The picture is protection all around God's people. A spear doesn't do that, but a shield does.
